title: PT1 practice exam (different from the real one)
note: Original questions and made-up engagements written for MyNextCert from TryHackMe's public PT1 topic list. Not real exam questions. Different from the real exam: real PT1 is a 48-hour hands-on engagement across web, network and Active Directory with a graded report, and no multiple choice. Each attempt here draws 20 multiple-choice questions and 5 simulated Pentest Lab engagements. All data is fabricated and nothing runs. Practice only in legal labs (TryHackMe, your own machines) with written permission. Domain weights are suggested study shares (verify).

q.q:
A tester with written permission runs this against the in-scope domain corp.lab:
$ dig axfr corp.lab @ns1.corp.lab
The reply lists 212 records, including vpn-old.corp.lab, hr-db01.corp.lab and a block of 10.10.30.x addresses. What does this show?
o: The domain is well protected, because every DNS reply is digitally signed and cannot be altered
Ordinary DNS replies are not signed unless DNSSEC is set up, and a full record dump is not a sign of protection.
Only public web servers are listed, so the result is harmless and needs no entry in the report
The records include a database host and private 10.10.30.x addresses, so internal systems are exposed.
The name server gives its whole zone to any requester, which leaks internal names and addresses
Right. A zone transfer is meant only for the organization's own secondary name servers. Allowing it for anyone is a misconfiguration that hands over the network map.
The query failed, because a normal DNS lookup returns one record and not a long list
A normal lookup returns one answer, but AXFR asks for every record in the zone, and here the server agreed.

q.q: The rules of engagement for a test of shop.example allow only passive reconnaissance on day one, meaning no traffic may be sent to the client's own servers. Which technique fits that rule?
o: Searching public certificate transparency logs for names issued under shop.example
Right. These logs are public records kept by third parties. Searching them sends nothing to the client, and they often reveal subdomains.
Guessing subdomain names from a wordlist by querying the client's own name server
Each guess is a query sent to the client's DNS server, so it counts as active traffic.
Requesting a zone transfer from the client's name server to see every record at once
This sends a request straight to the client's DNS server, which is active reconnaissance.
Running a ping sweep over the client's published address range to see which hosts reply
Ping packets go directly to the client's hosts, so this is active as well.

q.q: A default scan of 10.10.12.40 finishes in 4 seconds and shows only 22/tcp and 80/tcp open. The engagement lasts 48 hours and the host is expected to run a custom service. What is the best next scan?
o: No further scan, because two open ports means the scan is complete and the host is fully mapped
The default scan skips most of the port range, so a custom service on a high port would be missed.
A UDP scan of port 53 only, since DNS is the service most often left running on custom boxes
One UDP port tells you little. Covering the full TCP range gives far more information at this point.
The same top-1000 scan again with the fastest timing setting, to confirm the results
Repeating the same ports gives the same coverage, and very fast timing can even drop replies.
A scan of all 65,535 TCP ports, then version checks on open ones
Right. Default scans cover only the 1000 most common ports. A custom service often sits on an unusual port, so sweep them all first.

q.q:
A TCP scan of 10.10.12.41 reports:
22/tcp  open
80/tcp  closed
443/tcp filtered
What does "filtered" on port 443 tell the tester?
o: The port is open and the service on it is using encryption, so the probes were unreadable
Encryption does not change the scan state. An open port is reported as open.
Nmap got no clear answer, so a firewall or filter is probably dropping its probes
Right. "Filtered" means Nmap cannot tell whether the port is open, because something blocks or ignores the probes.
The service on that port is switched off and nothing is listening
A switched-off service with no filter normally sends a reset, which Nmap reports as closed, like port 80.
The host answered with a reset packet, exactly like port 80
A reset reply is what produces "closed". Filtered means no reply or a blocking message.

q.q:
Banner grabbing on a Linux server returns:
SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_7.2p2 Ubuntu-4ubuntu2.10
A junior tester writes "vulnerable to every OpenSSH 7.2 flaw" in the notes. What is the most accurate response?
o: The note is correct, because the upstream version number is the only thing that decides whether a flaw exists
Distributions back-port fixes, so the upstream number can overstate the risk.
Banners are always false, so the tester should ignore this one and every other banner
Banners are usually accurate and are a useful clue, but they must be verified.
OpenSSH 7.2 is old enough that it has no known flaws left to find
Age does not remove flaws. The issue is that patched packages can hide behind old numbers.
A suffix like this can mean back-ported fixes, so check the changelog before claiming a flaw
Right. Linux distributions often patch old versions without raising the upstream number, so the number alone proves little.

q.q: A web server sends "Server: Apache", but its error pages, header order and answers to malformed requests all look like IIS. How should the tester treat the banner?
o: As proof of the software in use, because a server cannot be set up to send a false name
Many servers let an administrator set a custom or false Server header.
As unproven, since headers can be edited; confirm with behavior-based fingerprinting
Right. Administrators can change headers. Behavior-based fingerprinting such as Nmap version probes is harder to fake.
As a critical finding, because the header and the real software do not match each other
Hiding or changing a banner is a hardening step, not a vulnerability.
As the only data needed, so the tester can skip the other checks and pick an attack path
One unverified clue is a weak basis for any decision.

q.q: A directory brute-force of http://10.10.8.15 reports all 4,000 wordlist entries as "200 OK, size 4521", including nonsense names like /zzqx91. What is the most likely cause, and what is the fix?
o: A soft 404: missing paths return the normal page, so filter by size
Right. A soft 404 sends 200 for pages that do not exist. Filtering out the common size or text leaves the real hits.
Every path exists, so the whole site is exposed and the finding should be rated critical
Random names like /zzqx91 almost certainly do not exist, and the repeated size points to one template.
The wordlist is corrupt, so the tester should switch to a much larger list and run it again
A larger list will repeat the same false positives.
A firewall is blocking the scan, so the tester should stop and report the host as unreachable
A blocking firewall produces errors, timeouts or resets, not a stream of 200 responses.

q.q:
With permission, a tester lists shares on a file server using an empty username and no password:
Sharename   Type
ADMIN$      Disk
C$          Disk
IPC$        IPC
Finance     Disk
The list came back with no login. Which entry deserves the first follow-up?
o: ADMIN$, because built-in administrative shares are always open to guests
Administrative shares need administrator rights. Anonymous users cannot normally open them.
IPC$, because it is the share where the finance documents are stored
IPC$ carries remote procedure calls between programs, not documents.
Finance, a custom data share an anonymous session may read
Right. ADMIN$, C$ and IPC$ are built-in defaults. A custom data share that an anonymous session can see is the interesting one.
None of them, since listing shares without credentials is not worth recording
Being able to list shares with no credentials is itself a misconfiguration worth writing down.

q.q: During an authorized scan, a tester finds a Jenkins server at http://10.10.8.4:8080 whose Script Console page opens without any login. Why is this a top-priority finding?
o: It only shows old build history, which is public information anyway
The Script Console is not a log viewer. It executes scripts.
The console runs code, so any visitor could take over the host
Right. Jenkins's Script Console is built to run commands, so open access amounts to remote command execution.
It reveals the Jenkins version number, which is a low-risk detail to mention at the end
The version is minor compared with open code execution.
It is only a risk when the server uses plain HTTP, and the fix is to switch to HTTPS
Encryption does not fix a missing login.

q.q: On an in-scope host, the Tomcat Manager page accepts the login tomcat / tomcat. Which description of this finding is best?
o: A software bug in Tomcat that the vendor must fix with a patch before the host is safe
Nothing is broken in the code. The product was left in its default setup.
A cross-site scripting issue in the login form
XSS involves injected script in a page, not a working login.
An informational note, because the page is only reachable from inside the network
Admin access to a server that can run uploaded apps is not informational, and inside access is a normal attacker starting point.
Default credentials on an admin interface that can deploy applications, a high-risk misconfiguration
Right. Vendor-default passwords are public, and the Manager can upload code, so the page leads to server control.

q.q: A customer portal in a lab shows an invoice at GET /api/invoices/10442 for the logged-in user. The tester, with permission, changes the number to 10443 and receives another customer's invoice. Which fix addresses the root cause?
o: Swap the sequential numbers for long random numbers and make no other change to the code
Random IDs are harder to guess, but anyone who learns one can still read it. The ownership check is still missing.
Remove the links to other invoices from each customer's page so they cannot be clicked
Hiding links does not stop someone from typing the address by hand.
Have the server check that the logged-in user owns each invoice before returning it
Right. This is an insecure direct object reference (IDOR). The server must verify ownership on every request.
Place a web application firewall rule in front of the API to block number changes in the path
A firewall cannot know which invoices belong to which user, and legitimate requests look the same.

q.q: An image importer in a lab app takes a URL from the user and fetches it from the server. A tester supplies http://10.10.3.7/admin, an address reachable only inside the client's network, and the response shows that internal admin page. Which flaw is this?
o: Server-side request forgery (SSRF), where the app is tricked into making requests for the attacker
Right. The server fetched an internal address on the user's behalf, reaching something the user could not reach directly.
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF), where a victim's browser is tricked into sending a request
CSRF abuses a logged-in user's browser. Here the server itself made the request.
SQL injection, where input changes the meaning of a database query
No database query is involved in what the tester did.
Clickjacking, where the page hides what the user is really clicking on
Clickjacking tricks users into clicking hidden page elements and has nothing to do with fetching URLs.

q.q: In a lab app, adding a single quote to the search box returns HTTP 500 and the text: "You have an error in your SQL syntax; check the manual ... near ''' at line 1". What does this response most strongly suggest?
o: The web server ran out of memory while handling the request
A memory fault would not name SQL syntax.
The page is protected against injection, because the app refused the unexpected character and said so
A protected app would treat the quote as data and return normal (possibly empty) results.
The input is placed into a database query unsafely, so SQL injection is likely
Right. A raw database error caused by one stray character shows the input reaches the query as code and not as plain data.
The browser blocked the request before it left the tester's machine, so nothing reached the server
The error text came from the server's database layer, so the request clearly arrived.

q.q: A search page copies whatever you type back into its response. Before trying special characters, which first step best follows good manual testing?
o: Send a harmless unique marker and see where it lands: body text, an attribute or a script
Right. Knowing the context tells you which characters matter, and you change one thing at a time with purpose.
Send many different test strings in one request to save time and see which one breaks the page
If several things change at once you cannot tell which one caused the result.
Switch off manual checks and rely only on an automated scanner for this page
Manual review is the point of this objective, and scanners miss context.
Skip the page, because input that is only reflected back to the same user is always safe
Reflected input is the basis of reflected cross-site scripting.

q.q: A login page replies "No such user" for unknown usernames and "Wrong password" for a real username with a bad password. What did this manual comparison reveal?
o: Strong authentication, since the page gives the user precise and helpful feedback
Specific messages help attackers. A single generic message is the safer design.
A SQL injection flaw, because the two replies come from two different database results
The behavior comes from different messages, not from query errors or injected input.
A session fixation flaw, because the page treats known and unknown names differently
Fixation is about a session ID that stays the same across login, which is not shown here.
Username enumeration: the two messages let an attacker confirm which accounts exist
Right. Different messages leak valid usernames, which narrows later password guessing. One generic message is safer.

q.q: A tester's proxy in Burp Suite captures all browser traffic, including requests to an analytics service and a CDN that the engagement scope does not list. What should the tester do?
o: Leave everything in scope so that no captured request is ever missed in the report
Third-party services belong to others, and you have no permission to test them.
Set the target scope to the client's hosts so no test traffic reaches the others
Right. Only the client's authorized hosts may be tested. Third-party services belong to other companies, and you have no permission to test them.
Send every captured request to Intruder so the whole session is tested in one go
This would also fire fuzzing at the third parties.
Turn off the proxy history so out-of-scope hosts are not visible
Hiding the data does not stop test traffic from reaching them.

q.q: After login, a cookie reads role=dXNlcg== . The tester pastes the value into Burp's Decoder and gets the word "user". Why does this matter?
o: The value is encrypted, so it cannot be changed by the user and is safe to trust
Base64 is not encryption. Anyone can decode it, as the tester just did.
Decoder proves the server is secure, because the value was readable only after conversion
Decoder converts formats. It makes no judgment about security.
The cookie can only be read by the server, which is why Decoder was needed
Cookies sit in the user's browser, so the user can see and edit them.
The role is only encoded, not protected, so the tester should check whether the server accepts an edited value
Right. Base64 is a reversible format, not encryption. If the server trusts the value, anyone could edit it to gain privileges.

q.q: A tester notes the session cookie before login is SID=a81f. After a successful login the cookie is still SID=a81f, now tied to the user's account. Which weakness is this?
o: A weak password policy that lets users pick short and easy passwords
Password rules are not involved in what the tester observed.
Session fixation: the app does not issue a new session ID after login
Right. If an attacker can plant a known ID before login, they inherit the session afterward. A fresh ID at login prevents this.
Missing HTTPS on the site, which is why the cookie can be read in transit
Transport encryption is a separate matter from keeping the same ID across login.
An expired certificate, which makes the browser reuse its old cookie
Certificates do not decide the value of a session cookie.

q.q: A user clicks Logout. The tester replays the old session cookie in a request to /account and the account page still loads. What is the finding?
o: Logout does not end the session on the server, so a stolen cookie keeps working
Right. Logout must destroy the session server-side. Deleting only the browser's cookie leaves it usable.
The logout button works correctly, because the page in the browser showed the login screen again
The old token still works, so the logout did not do its job.
The cookie is too short, which is why it can be reused after the user logs out
Length does not explain why a logged-out session still works.
The account page is public, so no login was ever required to view it
The page loaded because the old session was still valid, not because it is public.

q.q: An upload form only checks that the Content-Type header says image/png. Files land in /uploads/ inside the web root, where the server runs .php files. Which change reduces risk the most?
o: Trust the Content-Type header more strictly and reject any file whose header looks unusual
The header is chosen by the sender, so an attacker can set it to anything.
Limit uploads to 5 MB so large malicious files cannot be added to the folder
Small files can contain harmful code, so size limits do not address the cause.
Store uploads where scripts cannot run, and name the files on the server
Right. This stops uploaded code from running even if it slips in, and removes the attacker's control of the file name.
Rename the uploads folder to a long secret name so it is hard to find
Obscurity does not stop code from running once someone finds the path.

q.q: A download feature uses /get?file=report.pdf. Developers added a filter that removes the characters ../ once, in a single pass, yet a tester still reads files outside the folder. What is a stronger fix?
o: Drop the download feature, since filters can never work for file access
Safe downloads are possible with proper path checking.
Resolve the full path and confirm it stays inside the allowed folder
Right. Checking the final resolved path is reliable, whereas stripping strings can be beaten by overlapping text left after one pass.
Keep the filter as it is and blame the web server software for the exposure
The weakness is in the filter's design, not in the server.
Add more ../ patterns to the block list so every spelling of the sequence is covered
A longer block list still leaves gaps that clever spelling can slip through.

q.q: A signup form blocks usernames over 10 characters with a maxlength attribute and JavaScript, and holds a hidden field role=user. Which conclusion is correct?
o: The form is safe, because the checks run before the data is sent to the server
Checks that run on the user's machine can be skipped.
Hidden fields cannot be edited, so the role value is trustworthy as sent
Hidden only means not displayed. A proxy or the developer tools can change it.
JavaScript validation is enough once the script has been minified so it is hard to read
Minifying makes code harder to read, not impossible to bypass.
Any of it can be changed in the browser or a proxy, so only server-side checks count
Right. The browser is under the user's control. Servers must re-validate every value they receive.

q.q: In a lab app, the Delete User button is hidden for normal accounts. A tester sends DELETE /api/users/7 with a normal user's token and the account is removed. What is the finding?
o: A cross-site scripting flaw, since the page changed without the user pressing a button
No script injection was involved, only an unauthorized request.
A cosmetic page issue with no security impact
The page layout has nothing to do with the issue.
Broken access control: only the interface hides the action, and the API does not check who may delete
Right. Hiding a button is not a permission. The server must refuse the request.
A correct design, because the button stayed hidden for normal users
The design relies on the client and fails once the request is sent directly.

q.q:
An authorized scan of 10.10.20.30 returns, for port 445:
smb2-security-mode: Message signing enabled but not required
A tester is writing up risk. What does the line imply?
o: Relay risk: the server does not force signing, so forged traffic may be accepted
Right. Without required signing, an attacker in the network path may be able to relay authentication to this server.
SMB traffic to this host is fully encrypted end to end, so interception is not a concern
Signing proves a message was not altered. It does not encrypt, and here it is not even required.
The server blocks every connection that is not signed, so only trusted hosts can connect
That would be the result of requiring signing. This server only enables it.
The setting affects only printing and has no meaning for file sharing
The setting applies to all SMB traffic, including file sharing.

q.q: An engagement allows testing of SNMP on 10.10.20.50. A scan shows UDP 161 open and the community string "public" gives read access to the system description, running processes and network interfaces. What is the best recommendation for the report?
o: Make no recommendation, because read-only access cannot affect the security of the device
Read access leaks the device layout and running software, which is valuable to an attacker.
Recommend a fix only for printers, since other devices do not support SNMP
Routers, switches, servers and many other devices support SNMP.
Change the default string and move to SNMPv3 with authentication
Right. "public" is the well-known default. It works like a shared password sent in clear text in SNMPv1 and v2c.
Recommend closing port 161 on the TCP side, which stops SNMP from answering
SNMP uses UDP 161, so closing the TCP side changes nothing.

q.q: A tester has the lockout rule from the rules of engagement: accounts lock for 30 minutes after 5 wrong passwords in a row. The directory holds 400 usernames from an authorized enumeration. Which approach best respects the rule?
o: Try one common password against every account, then wait before the next round
Right. Spraying one guess per account stays under the lockout count, and the pause keeps counters from building up.
Try 1000 passwords against the first account until it works, then move to the next one
That locks the first account after 5 tries and may disrupt a real user.
Run guesses against all accounts in parallel as fast as possible and unlock them later
Locked accounts stop real staff from working, which breaks the rules of engagement.
Ask the help desk to disable lockout for the test without telling the client's security team
Changing controls in secret goes outside the agreed process. Any change needs written approval.

q.q:
An authentication log from a lab domain shows:
10:01 FAIL alice from 10.10.9.4
10:01 FAIL bob from 10.10.9.4
10:01 FAIL carol from 10.10.9.4
10:02 FAIL dave from 10.10.9.4
... (180 more users, one failure each)
How should a defender classify this pattern?
o: Ordinary brute force against one account, since all the failures come from one address
Brute force piles many tries on one account. Here each account sees just one attempt.
Normal behavior after a holiday, because many people mistype passwords together
180 different users failing once each from one address in minutes is not typical typing mistakes.
A denial-of-service attack, because the volume of requests is the main goal
The goal here is guessing accounts, and the volume is far too low to cause a denial of service.
Password spraying: one source tries few passwords across many accounts to avoid lockout
Right. One failure per account from the same source across a long list is typical of spraying, which avoids lockout.

q.q:
A tester finds the hash file below on a lab file server. Which choice names the sound way to handle it?
user1:$6$Qx9...$h4k2...
user2:$6$Zm1...$a7c9...
o: Post the hashes to a public cracking website to get the answer faster
Sending client credential data to third parties would break confidentiality.
Treat it as sensitive evidence, log where it was found, and crack only within scope
Right. The $6$ prefix shows salted SHA-512 hashes. Cracking offline is quiet, but it still needs authorization and careful handling.
Use the hashes against random outside servers to test if the passwords are reused there
Testing credentials against systems outside the scope is unauthorized.
Delete the file because hashes cannot be turned back into passwords
Hashes can be cracked by guessing, and the exposure is a finding.

q.q: A scan shows an FTP service banner "vsFTPd 2.3.4" on 10.10.20.60 in a lab. A tester wants to cite a known public flaw. What must the tester do before writing "exploitable" in the report?
o: Nothing more, because every host that shows this banner is certain to be vulnerable
A banner can be edited, or the flaw may be fixed while the number stays.
Launch the exploit against several other networks too, to see how widespread it is
Systems outside the scope are not yours to test, and the legal risk is serious.
Remove the finding, because old software versions are never a security issue
Outdated software with known flaws is one of the most common findings.
Confirm the version in scope; a banner alone does not prove the flaw
Right. A banner may be wrong or patched. The report needs evidence from a safe, authorized check.

q.q: A tester reviews a web server that prints a full stack trace and sends its "X-Powered-By: PHP/5.6.40" header. PHP 5.6 reached end of life years ago. Which severity reasoning is best?
o: Low only, since the header shows software details but nothing more
The version leak is minor, but the real problem is software that will never be patched.
Unsupported PHP gets no security fixes, and the stack trace gives attackers clues
Right. Unsupported software stays vulnerable forever. Verbose errors make attacking it easier.
Not a finding, because the site is online and works as expected
A working site can still run software that is dangerous.
Critical for the stack trace alone, since error pages never matter in any other way
A stack trace is a smaller issue than running unsupported software.

q.q: During an authorized test, a tester gets a shell on web server 10.10.20.5, which has a second network card on 172.16.5.0/24. The scope lists 10.10.20.0/24 and 172.16.5.0/24. The tester wants to scan a database host at 172.16.5.20 that is not reachable directly. What is the idea behind pivoting here?
o: Use the compromised server as a stepping stone to the network behind it
Right. Pivoting routes tests through a foothold host to a network that sits behind it. Both ranges are in scope, so it is allowed.
Copy the web server's files to the tester's laptop and test the files there
That is data collection and does not give a path to the second network.
Disable the web server's second network card so the networks are separated again
Changing the host's setup is not part of testing and could cause an outage.
Wait until the client reconfigures routing so the database is reachable
Waiting does not test anything, and the foothold already offers a path.

q.q: A tester pivots through 10.10.20.5 and discovers 10.10.50.8, an address NOT listed in the scope document. A scan could easily be run from the foothold. What is the right call?
o: Scan it quietly, because it is attached to a network in scope and so is covered
Scope covers listed addresses. Being reachable does not extend permission.
Scan it only with the lightest option, because gentle traffic cannot cause trouble
Even light traffic against an unlisted host is unauthorized.
Stop, note the host, and ask the client in writing whether to add it to scope
Right. Authorization is tied to what is written down. Reaching a host does not make it a permitted target.
Attack it and then ask for scope forgiveness in the final report
Testing first and asking later can break the contract and the law.

q.q:
Looking at a packet capture from a lab network, a tester sees a login that sends the following over port 80:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: intranet.lab
...
user=jlee&pass=Spring2026!
What should the report recommend?
o: Make the password field longer, since a long password is safe to send in clear text
Length does not help when the value is sent in plain text.
Require HTTPS so credentials cannot be read on the network path
Right. Plain HTTP sends the username and password readable. TLS protects them in transit.
Hide the login form from the public internet, since the exposure is only about the form
Hiding the form does not protect the traffic of those who can still reach it.
Change the form from POST to GET so the data shows less in the capture
GET puts data into the URL and logs, which is worse.

q.q: A tester on a lab switch wants to know why they cannot see other hosts' traffic even though their network card is in promiscuous mode. The lab uses switches, not hubs. What explains this?
o: The network card is faulty, so the driver should be updated before capturing again
Promiscuous mode works. Switching itself limits what arrives.
Encryption was switched on across the whole network, so captures are unreadable
Switches do not encrypt traffic. They only forward it selectively.
The tester's address is in another subnet, so the switch blocks all of it
Subnet membership does not decide what the switch forwards.
A switch sends frames only to the destination port, so you see just your own traffic
Right. Switches learn which address sits on which port. Capturing others' traffic needs a mirror port or similar authorized setup.

q.q:
A firewall test from outside shows:
PORT    STATE    SERVICE
22/tcp  filtered ssh
80/tcp  open     http
8443/tcp open    https-alt
The client's diagram says only 80 and 443 should be exposed. What is the best interpretation?
o: The firewall works perfectly, because port 22 is filtered and not open
A filtered port shows one rule working, but 8443 is open when it should not be.
Port 8443 is the same service as 443, so it is not worth mentioning
It is a different port that may host a different service, and it is not in the plan.
Port 8443 is exposed beyond the documented rules, so the firewall rules or the diagram need a review
Right. An open port that is not in the documented design points to a rule gap or an undocumented service.
Filtered ports mean the host is offline, so the scan is invalid
Filtered means probes got no answer or were blocked, while the host answered on other ports.

q.q:
The client says the guest Wi-Fi (10.10.77.0/24) is isolated from the server network. From a guest-Wi-Fi laptop, an authorized tester gets this:
$ nc -zv 10.10.10.5 1433
Connection to 10.10.10.5 1433 port [tcp/ms-sql-s] succeeded!
How should the tester record it?
o: Segmentation failure: guest users can reach a database port, so the filtering rules need review
Right. The isolation claim was tested and did not hold. The finding names the source, the target and the open path.
A pass, because the connection used an allowed port and so shows the firewall is working
An allowed path from the guest network is exactly what isolation should have prevented.
A scanner mistake, because Wi-Fi networks cannot reach any wired server by design
Wireless and wired segments are joined by routers, and a successful connection is real evidence.
Informational only, since a port that answers is not usable without a password
Reachability itself breaks the isolation promise, and the login can then be attacked.

q.q:
In an authorized lab review of corp.local, a tester lists accounts and notes:
svc_backup   DoesNotRequirePreAuth = True
svc_sql      ServicePrincipalName = MSSQLSvc/db01.corp.local:1433
jsmith       normal user, no special flags
Which account is exposed to AS-REP roasting?
o: svc_sql, because it has a service principal name registered on it
A service principal name makes an account a Kerberoasting target, which is a different attack.
jsmith, because every normal user allows this request by default
Pre-authentication is on by default, so normal users are not exposed unless someone turned it off.
svc_backup, because Kerberos pre-authentication is turned off for it
Right. With pre-authentication off, anyone can request data encrypted with that account's key and try to crack it offline.
None of the three, because Kerberos replies are always sent in clear text
Replies are encrypted. The weakness is that the key can be guessed offline when pre-authentication is off.

q.q: A defender reviewing the same lab sees that svc_sql runs a database and has the password Winter2024!, set eight years ago. Any domain user can request a service ticket for its SPN. What is the best fix?
o: A long random password, or a managed service account that rotates it by itself
Right. Kerberoasting cracks the ticket offline, so password strength decides the outcome. Managed accounts use long random passwords.
Stop domain users from requesting service tickets for any service on the network
Service tickets are needed for normal Kerberos use, so blocking them would break access to services.
Rename the account so an attacker cannot tell that it belongs to a service
The name is not what protects the ticket. The weak password is.
Add the account to Domain Admins so that it gets monitored more closely
Raising the privileges of an account with a weak password makes a cracked ticket far more damaging.

q.q: A tester with a low-privilege account queries a lab domain over LDAP and gets back every user, group and computer, including a Description field for one account that reads "temp pw: Autumn#26". What is the best description of this situation?
o: The query used a trick to read protected data that normal users should never be able to see
This is normal readable data. No special access was needed, which is exactly why secrets do not belong in it.
The Description field is encrypted by the server, so the tester must have broken in somehow
Description fields are plain text and readable by users.
The finding is minor, since the account is probably unused and could not be misused anyway
A working password in a readable field is a way in, whether or not the account is busy.
The directory shows most data to any domain user, so secrets in descriptions are exposed
Right. Most directory data is readable by authenticated users. A password in a description field is a common and serious mistake.

q.q: A tester wants to understand a lab domain before touching any host. Which source gives the clearest list of who belongs to Domain Admins using only an ordinary domain login?
o: Logging in to the domain controller and reading its local files by hand to find the list
This needs admin rights, which an ordinary domain login does not have.
An LDAP query for the Domain Admins group membership, using the ordinary login
Right. Group membership is readable by authenticated users, so this works with normal rights and sends only directory queries.
A UDP scan of every port on every workstation in the domain to look for admin names
A port scan shows services and says nothing about group membership.
A phone call asking the help desk to send the list, without a ticket or written permission
Social tricks are out of bounds unless the rules of engagement allow them, and they are not needed here.

q.q: BloodHound shows that the group Help Desk has GenericAll over the user account backup_admin, which is a member of Domain Admins. The tester is authorized to follow the path. What does GenericAll over that account mean?
o: Help Desk members can only read the properties of the account and nothing else about it
Reading is a much smaller right. GenericAll covers everything.
Help Desk members can log in to the domain controller console and no other computer
GenericAll is about control of the object in the directory, not about where a person may log in.
The right is harmless to the client, because only Domain Admins can ever make use of it
The right is held by Help Desk, a lower group, which is the problem.
Full control, including resetting backup_admin's password
Right. GenericAll is complete control over an object. Anyone in Help Desk could take over backup_admin and so reach Domain Admin.

q.q: A report line reads: "Group Contractors has WriteDACL on the OU Servers." Why should the client treat this as high risk?
o: The group can only change the OU's description text, which is a minor edit
That would be a write on one property. WriteDACL is about permissions.
The group can edit who has rights on the OU, so it can grant itself more access
Right. WriteDACL allows editing the permissions list. A group with it can give itself full control and reach what lies below.
The group can restart every server in the OU whenever it chooses to do so
Restarting a server needs rights on that server, which WriteDACL on the OU does not grant.
It is only worth a finding if the Contractors group already holds Domain Admin rights
Because the right lets the group raise itself, it matters even when the group looks harmless.

q.q: In a lab, a tester has the NTLM hash of a local administrator account from one workstation. Several other workstations share that local administrator password. Which defense best limits reuse of the hash?
o: A unique local administrator password on each machine, for example with Microsoft LAPS
Right. With a different random password on each machine, a hash taken from one machine is useless on the others.
A longer, more complex version of the shared password across all of the workstations
Reuse is the problem. The same hash opens every machine that shares the password, however long it is.
Switching off the firewall on the workstations so that logs are easier to read
Removing a firewall makes lateral movement easier.
Renaming the built-in administrator account to something unusual and hard to guess
A renamed account keeps the same hash and the same reuse issue.

q.q: A defender sees a Kerberos ticket that was first issued to a user on workstation A being used from workstation B's address to log on to ten servers, with no matching interactive logon on workstation B. Which technique should the defender suspect?
o: A forgotten password, since users often sign in to many servers by mistake
Ten server logons with no interactive logon is not an ordinary mix-up.
A printing problem in which the workstation keeps retrying its connections
Print retries do not produce logons to ten servers.
Pass-the-ticket, where stolen Kerberos tickets work without the password
Right. Tickets copied from memory let an attacker act as the user without the password, and the missing logon at the source fits.
Normal behavior for all Kerberos use, so no further review is required
Normal use has a matching interactive logon, so a gap deserves a look.

q.q: A tester in a lab holds a standard user account and finds in SYSVOL an old script that contains a Group Policy Preferences password stored with a published key. What is the right response?
o: Rate it informational, since the password is encrypted and so cannot be read by others
The encryption key is published by the vendor, so it is no real protection.
Report it as high risk, remove the stored password, and change the account's password
Right. That key is public, so anyone with domain access can read the password. Removing the file alone does not undo the exposure.
Use the account on other companies' networks to show how far the exposure could reach
Testing outside the engagement is unauthorized and illegal.
Ignore it, because the script is old and nobody uses it any more
An old file with a working password is still a way in.

q.q:
A tester sees this line in a domain controller policy review:
SeBackupPrivilege: Domain Users
The client asks why it matters. Which answer is best?
o: It only matters when the same users can also reboot the domain controller
Reading files needs no reboot right.
It is the default setting for every domain, so it can safely be left as it is
The privilege is normally limited to administrators and backup operators.
It allows users to change their own password without knowing the old one
That is a different setting and has nothing to do with backups.
It lets holders read any file, including credential stores, whatever the permissions
Right. Backup rights bypass file permissions, so holders can read sensitive files on the domain controller.

q.q: A BloodHound graph from an authorized lab review shows the shortest path from user lmoore to Domain Admins has three edges: MemberOf, AdminTo and HasSession. The client asks what to fix first. Which choice gives the most value?
o: Delete the BloodHound results, because they hold private data about the domain
The results are the evidence. Keep them secure and use them to fix the path.
Reset every account's password across the domain at once, so that the old path stops working
Resetting passwords does not remove the group membership or the local admin right that form the path.
Break the path at its weakest link, for example by removing the group's needless local admin rights on that computer
Right. Removing the link that gives local admin cuts the chain, and it is a cheap, low-risk change.
Disable logging for the three accounts so that the path is no longer recorded
Disabling logging hides activity and does nothing about the path.

q.q: A tester collected domain data from a lab with BloodHound, but the graph shows only 12 of an expected 400 computers. What should be checked first?
o: Whether the collection scope or network reach limited the data, so many objects never came back
Right. Incomplete data usually comes from the collection scope, rights or network reach, so check that before trusting the graph.
Nothing, because the client's number is probably wrong and the lab has just 12 computers
A big gap deserves a check against the source before the client's figure is doubted.
Whether the computers were switched on at that moment, since the graph shows only running ones
Domain data comes from the directory, not from machine power state.
Nothing, because a graph shows only the most important systems and hides the rest
BloodHound shows what was collected. It does not rank importance.

q.q: In an authorized lab, a scan shows a service banner "ProFTPD 1.3.5" on 10.10.40.12. A tester finds that Metasploit has a module for a flaw in that version. Which step belongs before running the module against the host?
o: Run it at once, since a module that exists for the version always succeeds against it
Success depends on configuration and patches, and an unplanned run could disrupt a live service.
Run it against the whole 10.10.40.0/24 range at once to find every vulnerable host fast
Testing every host in a range that includes systems outside the agreed list goes beyond permission and risks disruption.
Confirm the host is in scope and the module's effects are acceptable for the target
Right. Scope and impact come first. Some modules can crash a service, and the client must have agreed to that risk.
Skip the report entry, because only manual exploits count as evidence of a flaw
A framework result is valid evidence when it is recorded with the command, output and time.

q.q: A tester says: "The Metasploit module failed, so the service is not vulnerable." A senior tester disagrees. Which reasoning is strongest?
o: A failed run proves little; settings, versions or target state may explain it
Right. Exploits can fail for many reasons. A check of the version and conditions, or a manual test, is needed before clearing a service.
The senior is right only when the module was released within the past year or so
Age of the module does not settle whether the host is vulnerable.
A failed module is proof of safety, because frameworks test every known condition
Frameworks cover typical conditions only, and many flaws need unusual setups.
The tester should mark the host as patched in the report and move on right away
A failed exploit is not evidence of patching, so the report would claim something unproven.

q.q: A tester in a lab needs a shell from 10.10.40.15. The target sits behind a firewall that blocks all inbound connections to it but allows outbound traffic to the tester's address. Which kind of shell fits that firewall best?
o: A bind shell, where the target waits for the tester to connect in
A bind shell needs an inbound connection, and the firewall blocks it.
A shell on the firewall itself, which then reaches the target on the inside
Testing the firewall device is a separate matter and needs its own authorization.
No shell is possible whenever the firewall blocks inbound traffic to the host
Outbound rules still allow a connection from the target to the tester.
A reverse shell, where the target connects out to the tester
Right. Outbound traffic is allowed, so a connection started by the target gets through where an inbound one would be dropped.

q.q: A tester's lab shell can run commands, but pressing Ctrl+C closes it, arrow keys print odd characters, and a password prompt hangs. What does this tell the tester?
o: The target is protected by an antivirus tool that disables keys
Missing terminal features come from the shell type, not from antivirus.
The shell is not a full terminal, so upgrade it to a stable, interactive one
Right. A basic shell has no terminal handling. Upgrading it makes later steps reliable and avoids losing access by accident.
The network is dropping packets, so the tester should restart the whole engagement
One closed session does not mean the engagement or network is broken.
The account has no rights at all, so the tester has been fully locked out
The commands ran, so the account has some rights.

q.q: On a lab foothold, a tester needs to move a small analysis tool from the testing machine to the target. The target has no internet access, but it can reach the tester's address. Which method uses a standard tool already present and leaves the least change?
o: Install a remote access product on the target through its software store
Installing new software changes the target far more than needed.
Email the file to the target's user and wait for them to open it
Emailing a real user is not part of this test and needs separate approval.
Plug a personal USB drive into the server in the data center without telling anyone
Physical access is a different engagement and needs written permission.
Serve the file from the tester's machine and fetch it with a built-in tool
Right. This uses only what is already there and a connection the firewall allows.

q.q: After a test, a tester notices three tool files still on the lab target at C:\Windows\Temp. What is the correct handling?
o: Leave them in place, since the client will find and delete them one day
Leftover tools are a risk, and can be mistaken for a real attack.
Record names, hashes and locations in the notes, then remove them as agreed
Right. Cleanup is part of the work. The record lets the client confirm that everything was removed.
Rename them to harmless-looking names so that nobody notices them there
Disguising files hides your activity from the client.
Remove them quietly and say nothing, since the files are not part of the report
The report and notes must show what was placed and removed.

q.q: A rules-of-engagement document allows "temporary persistence for demonstration, removed at the end, with each change logged". A tester wants to leave a scheduled task on a lab server. Which approach is correct?
o: Use only the agreed name, log the details and remove it at the end
Right. This matches the allowed use. Logging lets the client's defenders tell your task from a real attacker's.
Create it with a name that looks like a Windows update, so it will not be noticed
A disguised name is deceptive and makes real cleanup harder.
Create it and leave it, since permission to add it also covers keeping it afterwards
The permission says the task must be removed at the end.
Skip logging it, because a note would make the report too long
Without a record, nobody can prove what is test activity and what is not.

q.q: During an incident review a defender sees a new service called "WinUpdateHelper" created at 02:14 on a file server, running a program from C:\Users\Public. What is the best next step?
o: Treat it as a normal Windows update, because the name says it is one
The name is only a label, and the odd location is a warning sign.
Delete it right away before collecting any details or screenshots
Deleting first destroys evidence of what it was and who created it.
Check change and test logs, then escalate it if nothing matches
Right. Persistence can be authorized testing or an attacker. The records settle which one it is.
Ignore it, because it was created at night when nobody was working there
Late-night activity is a reason to look closer.

q.q: On a Linux lab host, a tester notes that the account www-data can run "sudo /usr/bin/find" with no password. A junior asks why that matters. Which answer is best?
o: find only reads file names and so is safe to allow through sudo for a service account
It can also run commands on the files it finds.
find can start other programs, so allowing it through sudo may give root access
Right. Many common tools can run commands. When allowed through sudo they run as root, so the permission is much wider than it looks.
Sudo permissions do not matter on a web service account, only on a person's own login
Service accounts are common footholds, so their sudo rights matter a lot.
The rule is harmless, because running it needs no password and so is not a risk
No password makes it easier to abuse, not safer.

q.q: A Windows lab host runs a service "BackupSvc" as SYSTEM. Its executable path is C:\Program Files\Backup Tool\backup agent.exe with no quotes, and a normal user can write to C:\Program Files\Backup Tool\. Which fix best addresses the root cause?
o: Rename the service so that it no longer looks interesting to anybody who scans the host
The name does not change who can write to the folder.
Remove all users from the local administrators group of that host
Normal users are already not administrators, which is the point. The problem is the writable folder.
Turn the service off and on every night so the files are re-read
Restarting does not change who can write to the folder.
Restrict write access to that folder to administrators and quote the path
Right. A user who can write there can place a file that the service starts as SYSTEM. Fixing the permissions removes that option.

q.q: A tester finds that a lab file server also stores what looks like real employee records, outside the agreed target list. The rules of engagement name only 10.10.60.0/24. What should the tester do?
o: Copy the records to prove the finding is serious and delete them afterwards
Copying real personal data is a privacy and legal risk.
Read a few records to confirm they are real before deciding what to do
Opening real personal data goes beyond what was authorized.
Stop, avoid reading or copying the records, and tell the client contact now
Right. Real personal data outside scope must be handled with care. Stop and notify the client instead of looking further.
Say nothing, since the server is not on the list and so is not the tester's concern
The client has a duty to learn about exposed personal data, and prompt notice is the professional step.

q.q: The scope allows testing between 22:00 and 04:00 only. At 04:20 a tester finds a promising lead on a lab server and wants to continue. What is the right decision?
o: Stop, record the lead and ask the client in writing whether to extend the window
Right. The window is part of the authorization. Work outside it is unauthorized, so ask first and record the lead.
Continue for twenty more minutes, since a short overrun is unlikely to be noticed
An overrun is still unauthorized, and unnoticed does not mean allowed.
Continue and tell the client afterwards, because findings matter more than hours
Findings do not override the contract terms.
Delete the notes about the lead, so that nothing outside the window appears in them
Hiding the lead removes useful evidence and is dishonest.

q.q: A junior tester's draft finding reads: "The login page is bad and can be hacked." Which rewrite follows good report structure?
o: Keep it short and add the tools used, because the client wants to know which brand of scanner ran
The tool name tells the reader nothing about the flaw, its place or its impact.
Use technical words only, so that the report reads as expert work for the client's staff
Reports are read by managers and engineers alike, so plain wording is better.
State what the flaw is, the URL, how it was proven, and what an attacker could do with it
Right. A good finding names the flaw and where it is, shows the proof, and explains the impact in plain terms.
List every request the tester sent, in the order they were sent, with no summary
Raw logs belong in an appendix. The finding itself needs a clear explanation.

q.q: A tester proved SQL injection on a lab login. Which piece of evidence best lets the client's developers reproduce the finding?
o: The exact request, the affected parameter and the response that showed the flaw
Right. Developers need steps and data they can repeat. Request, parameter and response give them that.
A screenshot of the tester's desktop with the browser open in a corner of the screen
Without the request and response, nobody can repeat it.
A sentence saying the tester is certain, because of many years of experience in the field
Experience is not evidence. The report must show proof.
The full database contents copied from the lab server, attached to the report
Taking and sharing more data than needed is a privacy risk, and a few safe rows or none are enough to prove it.

q.q:
A tester has four findings. Which should rank first by risk?
A. Stored XSS in an admin-only page; planting it needs an account that can edit the page, and it runs as any admin who opens it.
B. Unauthenticated remote code execution on the public web server, easy to repeat.
C. Missing HTTP security header on the home page.
D. Weak password policy on an internal wiki with no sensitive data.
o: A, because it runs as every admin who opens the page and could take over the whole site
It needs an account that can edit the page first, so it is harder to reach than B, which needs no login at all.
C, because every page of the whole site is missing the header, so it has wide reach
Wide reach does not offset a very small effect.
D, because weak passwords are the main way that attackers get into networks
On a wiki with no sensitive data, the effect is small.
B, because it is easy to reach, needs no login and gives control of a server
Right. Risk combines impact and ease. B is the easiest to reach and the most damaging.

q.q: A tester has one finding they are proud of, a clever chain of five steps, but it only exposes a test account with no rights. Another finding is an open admin panel with default credentials on a production server. How should they be ordered?
o: Put the clever chain first, because it shows the most skill in the report
The report serves the client's risk picture, not the tester's pride.
Put the default-credentials panel first, because impact and ease decide the order
Right. Rank by impact and ease. An open admin panel is simple to abuse and affects production.
List them in the order they were found so the story is easy to follow
Discovery order says nothing about risk and could bury the key issue.
Leave the admin panel out, because defaults are too simple to count as real findings
Simple flaws that give control are often the most serious ones.

q.q: A report says "Apply security best practices" for a finding where a backup share allows anonymous read access. Which mitigation is the best replacement?
o: Buy a new firewall and place it in front of the server for added protection
A firewall does not change who can read the share from inside.
Train all staff on safe file sharing during the next security awareness month
Training does not close an open share and is not tied to the cause.
Move the backups to another server and leave the access rules as they are
Moving the data keeps the same weak access rules.
Disable anonymous access on the share; allow only the backup service account that runs it
Right. It names the cause (anonymous access), the place (the share) and a specific fix.

q.q: A tester found SQL injection caused by building queries from user text. The developer's fix: "Block the word UNION in the search box." Which comment best fits?
o: It is a complete fix, because attackers can only use that one word
Attackers have many ways to build a query, so a single blocked word does not stop them.
It treats a symptom; recommend parameterized queries as the root fix for the code
Right. Filtering words can be bypassed. Parameterized queries keep input as data, which removes the cause.
It is acceptable as long as the search box is hidden from the menu
Hiding a page is not a control.
It is the best fix, because filters are always stronger than changing the code
Changing how queries are built is stronger than a filter.

q.q: A 48-hour engagement has three targets. At hour 10 the tester has spent six hours on one box without progress, and the other two are untouched. What is the best decision?
o: Set a time limit, note what you tried, move on to other targets and return later
Right. A time box protects the whole engagement. Fresh eyes later often solve what hours of effort did not.
Stay on the box for four more hours, because it is the only target where you already have a lead
A lead is not progress, and two targets have had no time at all. Set a limit and move on instead.
Move on, and come back only at the end of the 48 hours with no notes so that you start fresh
Without notes you repeat the same steps. Write down what you tried so that the return visit is faster.
Ask other testers for the answers in an online chat so the box is quickly done
Sharing exam material is cheating and may break lab and exam rules.

q.q: A tester plans 48 hours for web, network and Active Directory work, then the report. Which plan is the most sensible?
o: Spend 47 hours testing and write the report in the final hour
A rushed report loses points and leaves out context.
Plan no breaks, because the sooner everything is found, the less time the report takes
Fatigue slows work and increases mistakes.
Split time per target, include sleep and breaks, and keep time for the report
Right. A written plan with limits and reserved report time prevents a rushed write-up.
Test only the target that looks easiest and skip the other two completely
The engagement scope covers all targets, so skipping two leaves large gaps.

q.q: Two weeks after a test, a client asks a tester which command found a particular host and when. The tester has no notes. What is the main lesson?
o: Keep notes only for findings and skip anything that did not work
Failed attempts also matter, because they show coverage and avoid repeated work.
Record commands, output, times and screenshots as you work
Right. Notes make the report accurate and back up claims if the client asks questions.
Write the notes from memory at the end of the engagement, when everything is clear
Memory fades quickly, and missing details can make findings unprovable.
Rely on the client's logs, since they will have everything anyway
Client logs may be incomplete, and they do not hold your reasoning.

q.q: While testing, a tester finds a file with real customer names in it. What should the notes contain about it?
o: A full copy of the file, saved to a shared drive so the whole team can read it
Copying real personal data to shared places increases exposure.
Nothing, since sensitive discoveries should never be written down
The client needs to be told, so the finding must be recorded safely.
The names of the customers, so that the client can contact each of them
The tester's job is to report, not to handle the client's customers.
The file's location and type, with the sensitive values hidden or redacted
Right. The notes show the finding without spreading personal data further.

q.q: A client's manager reads only the first page of a report. Which section should explain the attack path in terms the manager can act on?
o: A table of every open port found on every host in the whole network
Port lists belong in technical sections.
A glossary that defines each technical term used throughout the report
A glossary helps, but it does not tell the story.
An executive summary of the path, its business impact and the top fixes
Right. Managers need a short story: how things went wrong, what it meant for the business and what to do.
The raw tool output from the first day of testing, in the order it was produced
Raw output is evidence for the technical reader.

q.q: Which sequence best tells the attack path story for a lab compromise?
o: Foothold first, then each step with proof and root cause, up to the final access
Right. The story follows the order of events and ties each step to evidence and its cause.
The final access first, with no explanation of how it was reached by the tester
Without the steps, the reader cannot fix any weak link.
A list of the tools used, in alphabetical order, with their version numbers
Tools do not tell how the attacker moved or what let them.
Only the findings that the tester liked best, in any order that looks good
The path should be complete and honest.

q.title: Engagement 1: Brightcrate Shop web app
q.scenario: Brightcrate (a made-up online shop) hired you to test its public web server. Map the site, look for a way past the login, see how far an admin account can go, and write up what you can prove. Stay on the one server named in the brief.

rules: In scope: the web server 10.10.31.10 (shop.lab) only.
Out of scope: 10.10.31.20, the card payment gateway run by another company.
No denial of service and no deleting data.
Stop at proof: show you can run a harmless command, do not read customer data.
Report every finding with its severity and a fix.
Severity guide: critical = one flaw alone gives full server control, bulk data with no login, or a way across a network boundary.
High = real access that still needs another step or gives only a low-privilege login. Medium and low = helps an attacker but is no way in.
brief.note: Legal lab practice only: use these skills on TryHackMe, your own machines, or systems you have written permission to test. Every host here is made up.
brief.oosWhy: The payment gateway belongs to a card processor, not to Brightcrate. The signed scope covers the shop server only, so testing the gateway would be unauthorized, even if it sits on the same network.

The page printed a raw database error. The username goes straight into the query.

loot.why: Getting into the admin panel without a password proves the login query can be tricked. That is an authentication bypass, which is why the login finding is rated high.
Reading a file as the web server account proves the upload bug gives code execution. You stop here: proving it is enough, and you never need to read customer data.

checks.t: Run a version scan on the shop server
checks.why: -sV shows the exact software versions. You need them to judge which known bugs might apply.

checks.t: Find hidden folders with a wordlist
checks.why: A wordlist scan found /admin and /uploads, which no menu links to. Folders nobody links to are often where the weak spots are.

Unrestricted file upload gives code execution
Server software versions shown in HTTP headers
Cross-site scripting in the product search box
Default admin password still set on the panel login
SSH allows direct root login with a password
Directory listing enabled on the /admin folder
Apache CGI remote code execution (CGI is not enabled)
Login form has no CSRF token on any request
rems: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) for every database call
Check file type and content on the server, rename uploads and block scripts in /uploads
Hide version banners in the web server and PHP settings, then restart both
Add a CAPTCHA to the login form and lock the account after three failed attempts
Hide the admin link from the site menu so visitors cannot find the panel
Change the admin password every 30 days and enforce a longer minimum length
Block port 22 on the firewall and move SSH to a different port number
Turn on a web application firewall in front of the site, no code changes
Move the whole site to another hosting provider with a newer operating system

findings.title: SQL injection in the login form gives admin access
findings.rem: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) for every database call
findings.why: A raw database error and a password-free admin login show the username goes straight into the query. Admin access is serious but still needs one more step to run code, so high, not critical.

findings.title: Unrestricted file upload gives code execution
findings.rem: Check file type and content on the server, rename uploads and block scripts in /uploads
findings.why: Running code needs the admin login from the SQL injection first, so high on its own. Chained with the login bypass it gives full server control, so say so in the report. The fix is server-side checks: a filter in the browser can always be skipped.

findings.title: Server software versions shown in HTTP headers
